newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Tigers must earn their meat in China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tigers must earn their meat in China.

text.p: In modernising China where once-pampered state enterprises must show a profit or go under, even tigers need to make money to survive.

On a frozen, snow-covered wasteland in northern China, a Siberian tigress stared intently at a pheasant half-concealed in a deep drift of snow and pounced, swatting the bird with a paw as a small crowd of Chinese tourists broke into applause.

"Another one, another," cried the spectators, faces jammed against the protective bars of their bus, as the tigress devoured the bird. It was feeding time at the Siberian Tiger Park near Harbin, capital of northeast Heilongjiang province.
The tourists pay for each animal thrown to the tigers in the park's campaign to make the tigers earn their meat.
"It's cheap -- just 100 yuan ($12) for one pheasant," said the park's director, Liu Yincheng. At 40 yuan, chickens are cheaper, but the thrill of that hunt is too short-lived for entertainment.
In any case, the tigers soon tire of the game, hoping perhaps for something more substantial, such as one of the cows advertised at 1,500 yuan ($190) at the ticket office.
Few tourists come up with that kind of cash, which may help preserve the reputations of the tigers, currently under media criticism for losing their killer instincts.
ACCUSED OF GOING SOFT

Likening the tigers to China's lumbering state enterprises, the media last year said the endangered animals were losing those instincts during a life in captivity and needed to adapt to free competition.
Liu is trying to help them do just that.

"Under a market economy we are trying to protect the tiger in two ways, first to attract funds from society and second to use the tigers themselves to attract visitors and make money that way," Liu said.

Launched to increase numbers of the endangered Siberian tiger, Liu's Hengdaozi Breeding Centre was founded in 1986 under the umbrella of the Forestry Ministry with eight tigers and 13 million yuan ($1.5 million). By 1992, the centre had 69 tigers and a reputation for success.
SELLING TIGER PARTS
However, it gained notoriety amid reports that tiger parts were being used to fund the breeding programme.

In 1992, the government bowed to international pressure and imposed a ban on trade in parts of the endangered species, supporting the Convention of the International Treaty of Endangered Species (CITES).
Officials from the centre cried foul, complaining to the China Youth Daily that Beijing's ban on sales of tiger products had forced it to stop culling tigers and run into debt.
When the government refused to back down, the farm became just one of thousands of state-owned firms running at a loss.

The 36 square-km (22.5 mile) Siberian Tiger Park, opened last year, was one attempt to keep the operation profitable. Despite some success, the park alone does not bring in enough revenue to support the animals.

"Food for the 30 tigers here at the park and 50 in the breeding centre costs 3.0 million yuan ($361,000) a year. And that is only for food," Liu said. "With the park we can basically feed them, but we can't completely satisfy them."
ALTERNATIVE MONEY-SPINNERS
Liu hopes one day to be able to return the tigers to the wild. Until then, with each tiger eating 10 kg (22 lbs) of meat a day, life in China's free market is fraught with difficulties.
Liu has turned to other means to raise funds, such as a fox and mink farm. But sale of pelts from the park worries animal rights activists, already suspicious of Liu's activities.
"We definitely don't like what they're doing up there," said one Hong Kong-based activist, who declined to be identified.
Tourists admire Liu's solution for feeding his tigers.

"Other countries would not allow a situation where tigers went unfed," said visitor Zhang Lei. "Here we had to come up with our own ways of solving the problem. If no one did anything, the tigers would starve."
Liu understands his government's plight.

"Because we are a developing country, a lot of sectors need money and while there is money for environmental protection -- for example there is a lot of money for pandas -- we cannot completely depend on the government," he said.
"Our main goal is to keep the tiger alive. So this is a temporary solution to the problem of saving the tiger.

"To get the tiger back into the wild, we will need a lot more time and a lot more money than we can get by simply using the tiger's ability to attract tourists. To reach that goal, we will need more help from society and international help."
With only about 300 Siberian tigers surviving in the world, and only 20 in the wild in China, that help must come soon, said Liu.
